questions.stem: What is a mutagen?
options: An agent that increases the rate of changes to the DNA sequence
A protein that repairs damaged DNA after it has been replicated
A mutated allele that is passed from a parent to its offspring
A gene that controls the rate at which body cells divide
questions.explanation: Mutagens are physical, chemical or biological agents that raise the rate of mutation above the background rate of copying errors. DNA repair enzymes do the opposite, correcting damage.

questions.stem: How does ultraviolet (UV) radiation cause mutations in skin cells?
options: It adds whole extra chromosomes during cell division
It joins adjacent thymine bases into dimers that distort the DNA
It strips electrons from atoms, dissolving the whole DNA backbone
It converts every thymine base in the DNA into uracil
questions.explanation: UV is absorbed by DNA and links neighbouring pyrimidine bases, such as two thymines, into dimers; if these are not repaired, errors are made when the DNA is copied. UV is non-ionising, so it does not strip electrons from atoms the way X-rays and gamma rays do.

questions.stem: X-rays and gamma rays are forms of ionising electromagnetic radiation. How do they damage DNA?
options: They knock electrons from atoms, making reactive particles that can break DNA strands
They join adjacent thymine bases into dimers but are unable to break DNA strands
They add methyl groups to DNA that silence genes without altering the sequence
They damage only proteins, which then copy the DNA incorrectly in the next division
questions.explanation: Ionising radiation carries enough energy to remove electrons, producing ions and free radicals that break one or both DNA strands. Thymine dimers are typical of UV, and methylation is an epigenetic change rather than a mutation.

questions.stem: Which of these is a naturally occurring mutagen?
options: Haemoglobin, made in developing red blood cells
Aflatoxin, made by moulds on stored grains and nuts
Glucose, made by plants during photosynthesis in leaves
Insulin, made by beta cells in the pancreas after a meal
questions.explanation: Aflatoxins are toxins made by some Aspergillus moulds; they damage DNA and are linked to liver cancer. Glucose, insulin and haemoglobin are normal products of living cells and are not mutagens.

questions.stem: Radon is a radioactive gas that seeps naturally from some rocks and can build up in houses. Why does breathing it in increase the risk of lung cancer?
options: It is an infectious agent that inserts its genes into lung cells
It blocks the airways, so lung cells divide more slowly than normal
It emits radiation that damages DNA in the cells lining the airways
It replaces oxygen in the blood, starving lung cells of energy
questions.explanation: Radon and its decay products give off ionising radiation inside the lungs, which can break DNA and cause mutations that lead to tumours. It is a natural mutagen, not a pathogen.

questions.stem: Some chemical mutagens are flat molecules shaped like a base pair that slide in between the bases of DNA. What effect are they most likely to have?
options: Insertions or deletions during replication, causing frameshifts
Conversion of the DNA into RNA throughout the affected region
Removal of all the introns from the genes in the region
Permanent methylation of all the cytosines nearby
questions.explanation: These intercalating agents distort the helix so that DNA polymerase adds or skips bases when copying it, giving insertions or deletions that shift the reading frame. They do not convert DNA to RNA or remove introns.

questions.stem: A DNA sequence changes from ATG CCA TGA to ATG CGA TGA. What kind of point mutation is this?
options: Substitution
Insertion
Deletion
Translocation
questions.explanation: One base, C, has been replaced by another, G, and the length is unchanged, so this is a substitution. An insertion or deletion would change the number of bases.

questions.stem: An exon reads ATG GCT TAC GGA. After a mutation it reads ATG GCT ACG GA. What type of mutation is this?
options: A substitution that causes a missense change
An insertion that causes a frameshift
A deletion that causes a silent change
A deletion that causes a frameshift
questions.explanation: The T at the start of the third codon has been lost, so every base after it moves back one place and the codons downstream are read in a new frame. One fewer base means a deletion, not an insertion.

questions.stem: Which type of point mutation is least likely to change the function of a protein?
options: A nonsense substitution near the start of the gene
A single-base insertion near the start of the gene
A single-base deletion early in the gene
A silent substitution in an exon
questions.explanation: A silent substitution changes a codon to another codon for the same amino acid, so the polypeptide is unchanged. Nonsense mutations and frameshifts near the start usually destroy the protein.

questions.stem: In the beta-globin gene, a coding-strand codon GAG (glutamic acid) changes to GTG (valine), causing sickle cell disease. What type of mutation is this?
options: A frameshift insertion
A missense substitution
A nonsense substitution
A silent substitution
questions.explanation: One base is replaced and the codon now codes for a different amino acid, which is a missense mutation. A nonsense mutation would create a stop codon, and the gene length is unchanged, so there is no frameshift.

questions.stem: A substitution changes an mRNA codon from UAC (tyrosine) to UAA. What is the effect on the polypeptide?
options: The polypeptide is unchanged because the code is degenerate
Every amino acid after this point is changed
A stop codon forms, so the polypeptide is cut short
Tyrosine is replaced by a different amino acid
questions.explanation: UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends early and a shortened, usually non-functional, polypeptide is made: a nonsense mutation. Changing every downstream amino acid is the effect of a frameshift.

questions.stem: Why does a single-base insertion near the start of a gene usually cause more harm than a single-base substitution at the same position?
options: It alters the template strand but not the mRNA made from it
It adds one amino acid but leaves the rest of the chain unchanged
It shifts the reading frame, so every codon downstream changes
It always creates a stop codon exactly where the base is added
questions.explanation: Codons are read in threes from a fixed start, so adding one base changes every codon after it, usually giving a completely different sequence and an early stop codon. A substitution affects only one codon.

questions.stem: A deletion removes exactly one codon, three adjacent bases, from the middle of an exon. What is the most likely effect on the polypeptide?
options: The polypeptide is unchanged because deletions of three bases are silent
One amino acid is missing, but the rest of the sequence is unchanged
Every amino acid after the deletion is changed by a frameshift
The polypeptide ends at the deletion because a stop codon forms
questions.explanation: Removing a whole codon keeps the reading frame, so one amino acid is lost and the rest is normal; the most common cystic fibrosis variant is a three-base deletion that removes one amino acid. Losing one amino acid can still change folding, so it is not silent.

questions.stem: A coding strand reads 5' ATG TGG AAA 3', coding for Met-Trp-Lys. A substitution changes the second codon to TGA. The mRNA codon UGA is a stop codon. What is made?
options: Methionine only, because translation stops
Met-Trp-Lys, because the change is silent
Met-Lys, because the second codon is skipped
Met-Lys-Trp, because the codons are reordered
questions.explanation: The mRNA becomes AUG UGA AAA, so translation stops after methionine: a nonsense mutation. Ribosomes do not skip a stop codon and carry on, so lysine is not added.

questions.stem: A missense mutation changes one amino acid in the active site of an enzyme. Why might the enzyme stop working?
options: The active site's shape or charge changes, so the substrate no longer binds
The enzyme becomes much longer than normal, so it cannot fold at all
The enzyme's mRNA can no longer pass through the nuclear pores
The gene for the enzyme can no longer be transcribed by RNA polymerase
questions.explanation: The R group of the new amino acid may have a different size, charge or polarity, altering the active site so it no longer fits or binds its substrate. A missense change swaps one amino acid without changing the chain length.

questions.stem: A substitution occurs in the middle of an intron, well away from the splice sites. Why is it unlikely to affect the protein?
options: Introns are never transcribed by RNA polymerase
Introns are found only in the DNA of the mitochondria
Introns are removed from pre-mRNA before translation
Introns are translated, but their amino acids are removed
questions.explanation: Introns are transcribed but spliced out of pre-mRNA, so a change deep within one does not reach the mRNA that is translated. A change at a splice site, however, can alter which sequences are kept.

questions.stem: A section of a chromosome breaks off, turns through 180 degrees and rejoins in the same place. What is this mutation?
options: Translocation
Duplication
Deletion
Inversion
questions.explanation: In an inversion the segment is reversed but stays on the same chromosome. In a translocation the segment moves to a different, non-homologous chromosome.

questions.stem: In chronic myeloid leukaemia, part of chromosome 9 and part of chromosome 22 swap places. What type of mutation is this?
options: Duplication
Non-disjunction
Translocation
Inversion
questions.explanation: Exchange of segments between non-homologous chromosomes is a translocation; this one forms the Philadelphia chromosome and a fused gene that drives cell division. Non-disjunction changes the number of chromosomes, not their structure.

questions.stem: A chromosome with the gene order A B C D E F G is found as A B C D E F E F G in one person and as A B E F G in another. Which mutations are these?
options: A deletion in the first and a duplication in the second
A translocation in the first and an inversion in the second
A duplication in the first and a deletion in the second
An inversion in the first and a translocation in the second
questions.explanation: In the first, segment E F appears twice, which is a duplication; in the second, C D is missing, which is a deletion. An inversion would show a segment in reverse order, such as A B E D C F G.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares point mutations and chromosomal mutations?
options: Point mutations alter many genes at once; chromosomal mutations alter only a single base pair
Point mutations are visible in a karyotype; chromosomal mutations are too small to be seen in one
Point mutations are always inherited by offspring; chromosomal mutations are never inherited
Point mutations alter one or a few bases; chromosomal mutations alter large sections with many genes
questions.explanation: A point mutation changes the sequence at one site within a gene, while a chromosomal mutation changes the structure or number of chromosomes and can affect many genes. Only large chromosomal changes are visible in a karyotype.

questions.stem: Which type of mutation could be seen in a karyotype?
options: A translocation of a large segment
A substitution of one base in an exon
A silent mutation in a gene for an enzyme
A single-base deletion causing a frameshift
questions.explanation: A karyotype shows whole chromosomes under a microscope, so only changes in number or in large segments are visible. Point mutations change single bases and need DNA sequencing to detect.

questions.stem: What is non-disjunction?
options: Failure of homologous chromosomes or chromatids to separate in cell division
Breaking and rejoining of a chromosome segment in the reverse direction
Exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids in prophase I
Joining of two different chromosomes end to end during fertilisation
questions.explanation: When homologues fail to separate in meiosis I, or sister chromatids in meiosis II, gametes end up with an extra or a missing chromosome. Exchange of segments is crossing over.

questions.stem: A karyotype shows 45 chromosomes, with a single X chromosome and no Y. What condition is this, and how did it arise?
options: Down syndrome, from a gamete with an extra copy of chromosome 21
Turner syndrome, from a translocation joining the X and Y chromosomes
Turner syndrome, from a gamete with no sex chromosome after non-disjunction
Klinefelter syndrome, from a gamete with an extra X after non-disjunction
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome (45,X) results when one gamete carries no sex chromosome because of non-disjunction and fuses with a normal X-bearing gamete. Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY.

questions.stem: A karyotype shows 47 chromosomes, including the sex chromosomes XXY. Which statement is correct?
options: It shows a translocation that has joined an X chromosome to a Y
It shows Klinefelter syndrome, from non-disjunction of sex chromosomes
It shows Turner syndrome, from the loss of one of the X chromosomes
It shows Down syndrome, from an extra copy of chromosome 21
questions.explanation: 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome: an egg or sperm carried an extra sex chromosome after non-disjunction. The person has a Y chromosome, so develops as male.

questions.stem: Non-disjunction of one homologous pair occurs in meiosis I, and meiosis II is normal. How many of the four gametes have an abnormal chromosome number?
options: Two of the four
One of the four
No gametes
All four
questions.explanation: If a pair fails to separate in meiosis I, one cell gets both homologues and the other gets neither, so all four gametes are n + 1 or n - 1. Non-disjunction in only one cell in meiosis II affects two of the four gametes.

questions.stem: Chromosomes in a karyotype are arranged in homologous pairs by size and banding. How does this arrangement reveal a trisomy?
options: The trisomy shows as a gap in the banding of one chromosome
Three matching chromosomes appear where there should be a pair
The extra chromosome is stained a different colour from the rest
The trisomic chromosome is always twice the normal length
questions.explanation: Because homologues match in size, centromere position and banding, an extra copy is obvious as a set of three. Stain colour and length do not change with trisomy.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a somatic variant and a germline variant?
options: A somatic variant affects whole chromosomes; a germline variant affects single bases
A somatic variant is always harmful; a germline variant is always beneficial
A somatic variant arises in a body cell and is not inherited; a germline one can be
A germline variant arises in a body cell and is not inherited; a somatic one can be
questions.explanation: Somatic variants occur in body cells and are passed only to the cells descended from that cell, so they are not inherited by offspring. Germline variants are in gametes or the cells that make them, so they can pass to the next generation.

questions.stem: A long-term smoker develops a lung tumour caused by mutations in lung cells. Could these mutations pass to children the smoker has afterwards?
options: No, because they are somatic mutations in lung cells, not in gametes
Yes, because every mutation in the body is copied into the gametes
Yes, but only to children conceived after the tumour began to form
No, because tumour mutations are always repaired before reproduction
questions.explanation: The mutations are in somatic cells of the lung, so the gametes do not carry them and children cannot inherit them. Tumours exist precisely because some mutations are not repaired.

questions.stem: A tumour usually forms only after several mutations build up in one cell line, for example in genes that control cell division. Why is cancer more common in older people?
options: Older people inherit extra mutations from their children through shared blood
Cell division stops completely in old age, so any tumours grow without control
Somatic mutations accumulate over a lifetime, so several in one cell become more likely
Germline mutations switch on only after middle age, in every cell of the body at once
questions.explanation: Every division and every exposure to mutagens adds a small chance of mutation, so with time the chance that one cell lineage gains all the changes needed for a tumour rises. Germline variants are present from conception, not switched on later.

questions.stem: A person inherits one faulty copy of a tumour suppressor gene such as BRCA1 through the germline. Why is their risk of some cancers much higher?
options: The faulty allele makes a protein that directly breaks the DNA in breast and ovary cells
A germline mutation doubles the rate at which all of the person's body cells divide
Every cell already has one faulty copy, so a single further mutation can disable the gene
The faulty copy is dominant at the cell level and causes tumours in every cell from birth
questions.explanation: Tumour suppressor genes usually need both copies disabled before a cell loses control; with one faulty copy inherited, only one somatic mutation is needed in any cell. Most people with the variant are born healthy, so it does not cause tumours in every cell.

questions.stem: Why are germline variants, rather than somatic variants, a source of new genetic diversity in a population?
options: Somatic variants cannot change the base sequence of DNA
Somatic variants occur only in plants, never in animals
Only germline variants pass to offspring and enter the gene pool
Germline variants are always beneficial to the organism
questions.explanation: A variant must be in a gamete to be inherited and so change allele frequencies over generations. Somatic variants are real changes in DNA, but they end with the individual.

questions.stem: What is a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)?
options: A sequence of several bases repeated many times at one locus
A variation at one base position that is common in a population
A large deletion of a chromosome segment found in only one person
A change in the number of whole chromosomes in a cell
questions.explanation: A SNP is a difference of a single base at a particular position in the genome, present in a noticeable proportion of a population. Repeated sequences at a locus are short tandem repeats, used in DNA profiling.

questions.stem: In a study, a particular SNP variant is found in 30% of people with a disease and in 10% of people without it. What does this show?
options: The SNP protects against the disease, because most of the patients lack it
The SNP plays no part in the disease, because 70% of the patients lack it
It shows an association with the disease, not proof of cause
The SNP causes the disease in every single person who carries the variant
questions.explanation: The variant is three times as common in people with the disease, so there is an association, but the SNP may simply be inherited alongside a causal variant or be one of many risk factors. Most carriers never get the disease, so it does not cause it in every carrier.

questions.stem: Why might a SNP outside any gene's coding sequence still be useful when testing for a disease risk?
options: It may be inherited along with a nearby disease-causing variant, so it acts as a marker
SNPs outside genes are translated directly into the proteins that cause the disease
SNPs outside genes change the number of chromosomes passed on in the gametes
It changes the amino acid sequence of every protein made by the cell
questions.explanation: A SNP close to a disease-causing variant on the same chromosome is rarely separated from it by crossing over, so the two are usually inherited together and the SNP flags the risk. Non-coding DNA is not translated.

questions.stem: A direct-to-consumer SNP test reports that a person has a 'low genetic risk' of type 2 diabetes. Why could this result be misleading?
options: SNP tests measure blood glucose levels rather than any part of the DNA
Risk depends on many genes and on lifestyle, and the test reads only some SNPs
SNP tests read the whole genome, so the risk estimate is always certain
Type 2 diabetes is caused by a single SNP, which these tests cannot detect
questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes is influenced by many genetic variants of small effect and strongly by diet, exercise and weight, so a low genetic score does not mean low overall risk. These tests read selected SNPs, not the whole genome.

questions.stem: Most people in the large SNP databases used to estimate disease risk have European ancestry. What is one consequence for diagnostic testing?
options: Risk estimates may be less accurate for people of other ancestries
People of other ancestries carry no SNPs that can be tested for
Risk estimates become more accurate for people of other ancestries
Tests can detect SNPs only in people of European ancestry
questions.explanation: SNP frequencies and their links to disease differ between populations, so estimates built mostly from one group may not transfer well to others. Everyone carries SNPs, and the tests can detect them in anyone.

questions.stem: Which is a genuine limitation or constraint of SNP databases used in diagnostic medicine?
options: Concerns about privacy and who, such as insurers, can access genetic data
Each person's SNPs change every year, so stored data soon become outdated
SNPs are found only in mitochondrial DNA, so the data cover very few genes
The databases can only hold data from people who already have a disease
questions.explanation: Genetic data identify a person and their relatives, so storing and sharing them raises privacy and discrimination concerns. A person's germline SNPs are fixed from conception and are found throughout the nuclear genome.
